title: Tensioning fabric in a frame
subtitle: How to get even, stable tension on a scroll frame or slate frame.
excerpt: Even tension across the whole cloth prevents distortion as stitching fills the design area. The lacing method on a scroll frame and the bracing method on a slate frame both achieve this; the key is tightening evenly from the centre outward.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Frame mounting and tensioning methods.
Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Internet Archive. Stretcher frame technique.

glossaryTerms.definition: Strong thread or fine string run through the fabric edges and around the side bars of a scroll or slate frame to keep the cloth taut from side to side while the top and bottom rollers hold the warp direction.

content.text: Even tension on a frame keeps a large design from distorting as the stitched area grows. On a scroll frame, the cloth is attached top and bottom to the rollers and then laced through the sides. On a slate frame, the cloth is braced to each side bar individually. Both methods follow the same principle: start from the centre of each side and work outward, adjusting tension evenly.

items.name: Strong thread or fine string for lacing

content.text: Mounting and tensioning on a scroll frame
Turn a hem or sew a length of tape along the top and bottom edges of the fabric. This is where the fabric attaches to the rollers.
Stitch the top hemmed edge to the webbing on the top roller, starting from the centre and working outward to both ends.
Tighten the side bars until the fabric is taut from top to bottom but not distorted.
and lace through the selvedge or hem of the side edges, looping around the side bar every 2 to 3 cm.
Pull the lacing firm but not tight enough to dimple the cloth. Tie off at each end. The cloth should feel like a drum.

items.symptom: The cloth is tight on one side and loose on the other
items.cause: Lacing was started at one end and pulled in one direction only.
items.fix: Start lacing from the centre of each side and work outward, adjusting the tension equally on both sides before tying off.

items.symptom: The fabric distorts as stitching progresses
items.cause: The cloth was not square when mounted, or the lacing tension was uneven.
items.fix: Remount. Use a right-angle ruler or the grid on a cutting mat to check the grain is square before lacing.

content.text: Frame tensioning underpins all professional counted work and goldwork. It stops distortion building up over a long project. This matters most in Hardanger, where withdrawn threads pull the cloth out of square when tension is poor.
